questions.q: For ordinary tabular business data, which is the usual strong default after a simple baseline?
questions.explain: Gradient boosting typically matches or beats neural networks on tabular data with less tuning, as the lesson's experiment and the 2022 Grinsztajn et al. benchmark both suggest.

questions.q: In the lesson's experiment, why did boosting beat the MLP on the churn-style data?
options: The MLP had too few neurons to represent anything
Churn followed threshold rules, which trees split on naturally, and trees are less bothered by irrelevant columns
questions.explain: Rules such as tenure under 12 months are thresholds, which trees handle directly, and the 8 noise columns hurt the network more than the trees.

questions.q: On the smooth/rotated dataset the MLP scored 0.880 and boosting scored 0.600. What does this illustrate?
options: Networks learn combinations of features, which helps when the boundary is diagonal or smooth in many features
questions.explain: Trees split along one feature at a time, so smooth combinations of many features are hard for them, while a network can learn such combinations.

questions.q: Why should you be careful about over-reading the two synthetic datasets in the lesson?
options: They are illustrative: we wrote the generating rules, so each favors one model type by construction
questions.explain: The synthetic sets demonstrate mechanisms (thresholds versus smooth combinations); real data has to be tested on its own.

questions.q: Which of these is a case where a neural network is the clear default choice?
options: A 500-row spreadsheet of customer ages and incomes
A small table of monthly sales totals
questions.explain: Unstructured data such as images, audio and text has no hand-made columns, so learned features (and transfer learning) are where networks excel.
